newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavarian minister says EMU criteria must be strict.
newsitem.headline: Bavarian minister says EMU criteria must be strict.

text.p: A leading Bavarian state minister said on Saturday that European economic and monetary union (EMU) should not go ahead unless all participants strictly met the Maastricht convergence criteria.

Bavarian Finance Minister Erwin Huber, who is a close political ally of German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, told the Berliner Morgenpost newspaper that only if all EMU first rounders met the criteria "to the same degree" would a stable euro be guaranteed.

It would not be enough for Germany to meet the three percent ratio of deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) reference target stated in the Maastricht Treaty if other countries were to overshoot it, he said.
"From our point of view, that means that France must reach three in the sense of 3.0," Huber was quoted as saying.
The newspaper said Huber was reacting to a speech by France's new socialist prime minister, Lionel Jospin, who laid out his economic policy programme before parliament on Thursday.
Jospin made no reference to the three percent deficit criteria, nor did he give any indication how France would go about covering an expected revenue shortfall.

Some independent analysts say France's deficit-to-GDP ratio is likely to be as high as 3.6 percent in 1997 -- the reference year for EMU qualification. Many economists also say Germany is unlikely to achieve a 3.0 percent deficit ratio.
Huber, a member of the Christian Social Union (CSU) which Waigel leads, made clear that if strict convergence were not achieved EMU should be delayed, the newspaper said.
"The principle that stability comes before the timetable must apply across Europe," he said.
